extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, manuscript preparers, and typesetters
extracted.subtask_description: Style and preparation rules for mathematical notation, symbols, and for quoting/dialogue in manuscripts intended for publication; guidance covers how to mark ambiguous math copy for typesetters and detailed conventions for quoting, block quotations, punctuation, capitalization, poetry extracts, and permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark ambiguous mathematical symbols for typesetter
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs and symbols that could be misread by the typesetter should be clearly identified on a paper manuscript by marginal notations or in a separate list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide marginal notations or a separate list naming ambiguous symbols (e.g., whether a handwritten x is xk or XK or Xé). See examples in figures and tables; only identify symbols if badly written or rendered (note b). Illegible handwriting and unidentifiable signs can reduce composition speed and cause costly corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify commonly confused math characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain letters, numbers, and symbols can easily be misread, especially when Greek, Fraktur, script, and sans serif letters are handwritten rather than typed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided tables (e.g., table 12.4) to note confusions such as l vs numeral 1, t and i similarity, v vs nu, Greek letters vs Latin lookalikes. Note 'el' for lowercase L in some fonts but leave numeral unmarked; avoid using '@' if '/' is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space around binary operation signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave medium space before and after binary operation signs (=, <, ∈, ±, ×, +, −, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add space when such signs are used to modify symbols or expressions (e.g., -3, +1) or when operations appear as subscripts or superscripts. For the multiplication symbol, use a centered period as the multiplication dot, allowing medium space on each side, but do not show space around a center dot in chemical formulas (CO3·H2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use printer's term for partial differential
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the printer’s term “round dee” for the partial differential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer wording that is easier for printers to interpret when marking manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime, superscript, and subscript distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use apostrophe for prime if no prime available; in handwritten formulas, take care to distinguish prime from superscript 1 and comma from subscript 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark clearly to avoid confusion between similar marks (prime vs 1 vs comma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen, en dash, em dash, and minus sign usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two hyphens for em dash; no space on either side (except in LaTeX contexts where a double hyphen produces an en dash). For minus (subtraction) sign, leave medium space on each side; omit space after sign if representing a negative quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphens used as em dashes may be changed to em dashes and spacing adjusted; hyphens may be changed to en dashes in number ranges. Apply consistently and mark preferences when necessary (e.g., LaTeX conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication dot formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use centered period for multiplication dot, allowing medium space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show space around a center dot in chemical formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author preference declarations for ambiguous forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for forms that may be ambiguous (e.g., forms of o/O notation or different forms of certain symbols) should be specified by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two similar forms may occur together (e.g., O(x) and o(x)), specify preferred form in manuscript; more commonly used forms noted in table where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin letter italics default
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin letters in mathematical expressions will automatically be set in italics unless marked otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only indicate non-italic where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only mark badly written symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Only if symbols, letters, or numbers are badly written or rendered in the manuscript is it necessary to identify them for the typesetter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-marking; mark only when handwriting or rendering creates ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give credit and obtain permissions for quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should give explicit credit to the source of quoted words or ideas and may need written permission for certain uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permission may be required for more than a line or two of a poem or song lyric in copyright; for prose quotations of more than about three paragraphs or many short passages from a copyrighted work; or for any excerpt from certain unpublished materials (letters, email, interviews). Cite sources formally in notes or parentheticals and consult chapter 4 for permissions detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between quoting and paraphrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should decide whether direct quotation or paraphrase will be more effective; too many quotations with too little commentary can distract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrase when the original contains errors or when a quotation would be lengthy; silent corrections may be permitted for obvious typographic errors (see 'sic' guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not quote common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly known or readily verifiable facts can be stated without quotation or attribution unless the wording is taken directly from another source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure authors are absolutely sure of unattributed facts; editors should flag anything suspicious. Proverbs and familiar expressions usually need no quotation or attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure meticulous accuracy of quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should check every direct quotation against the original (or a careful transcription) before manuscript submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript editors may spot-check quotations but are not typically expected to confirm every source; it is far quicker for authors to transcribe accurately during writing than to correct later (see also editorial responsibilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible changes to quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although wording should be reproduced exactly, certain changes are generally permissible to make a passage fit the syntax and typography of surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible changes include (1) changing single to double quotation marks (and vice versa) and adjusting punctuation accordingly; (2) changing en dashes/hyphens used as em dashes to em dashes and adjusting spacing; (3) changing the initial letter to capital or lowercase to fit syntax; (4) altering or omitting terminal punctuation to fit surrounding text (retain ? or ! when still applicable); (5) omitting original note reference marks unless omission affects meaning—if retained, distinguish added references; (6) silently correcting obvious typographic errors unless the source's idiosyncrasies should be preserved—if modernized, inform readers in note or preface; (7) modernizing archaic characters like the long s when appropriate, but be cautious with historical texts (do not change u/v or i/j without subject-area expertise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible changes to typography and layout of quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of typography and layout may be changed to assimilate a quotation to surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed changes: (1) change typeface/font to match surrounding text; (2) set full-capital words in small caps if preferred; (3) move speakers' names in drama/dialogue from centered to flush left; (4) convert underlining in quoted manuscripts to italics unless underlining is integral; (5) in quoted correspondence, adjust paragraph indents and position of salutations/signatures. See related sections for poetry and block-quotation specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run-in versus block (set-off) quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted text may be run in to surrounding text (in quotation marks) or set off as a block quotation (not enclosed in quotation marks, always starting a new line and usually indented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length usually decides: short quotations, especially fragments, should be run in; about 100 words or more can generally be set off as a block quotation. Quotation of two or more paragraphs, correspondence, lists, and material requiring special formatting are best set off. When comparing multiple quotations as entities, prefer setting them all as block quotations even if short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilate quotations logically and grammatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase surrounding sentences so quoted words fit logically and grammatically as if there were no quotation marks; quote only as much as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate tenses and pronouns appropriately; use brackets sparingly when adjusting quoted material for integration; example transformations provided. Bracketed adjustments should be used sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation with quotations (commas, commas when inverted or interrupted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma after verbs like said, replied when identifying a speaker; when quotation comes first in an inverted sentence, a comma is usually required at the end of the quotation unless it ends with ? or !; an interrupted quotation requires two commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a quotation is subordinated or integrated into the sentence, no comma is needed (e.g., Fish observed that “what [the students] did...”); see sections on other punctuation such as colon use.

rubrics_metrics.name: No comma when quotation is syntactic part of sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation introduced midsentence forms a syntactical part of the surrounding sentence, no comma or other mark of punctuation is needed to introduce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Donovan made a slight bow and said he was “very glad.” One of the protesters scrawled “Long live opera!” ...

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon to introduce quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation is introduced by an independent clause (a grammatically complete sentence), a colon should be used to introduce the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A colon may also be used sparingly in place of a comma to introduce a quotation for emphasis or when introducing quotations of more than one sentence; block quotations may instead be preceded by a period unless introduced by 'as follows' or similar wording that requires a colon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial capitalization adjustments for quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial letter in a quoted passage may be changed to capital or lowercase to conform to the surrounding syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such adjustments may be done silently in most works, but in legal writing or close textual commentary it may be obligatory to indicate changes by brackets. For run-in quotations that form a syntactical part of the sentence, begin with a lowercase letter even if the original begins with a capital; when the quotation has a more remote relation, retain capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brackets to indicate changes in capitalization where required
rubrics_metrics.description: In some legal writing, close textual analysis, or other contexts, it is considered obligatory to indicate any change in capitalization by brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ this practice consistently throughout the work where appropriate (examples given with bracketed capitals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Block-quotation formatting (multiparagraph and beginning-in-text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted material of more than a paragraph should be set off as a block quotation; multiparagraph block quotations should generally reflect paragraph breaks of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the first paragraph quoted includes the beginning of that paragraph, it need not start with a first-line indent; subsequent paragraphs in the quotation should be indicated by first-line indents or extra line space. A long quotation may begin with a few words run in to the text only when text intervenes between the quotation and its continuation; otherwise set off the whole passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text following a block quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the text following a block quotation is a continuation of the introductory paragraph, it begins flush left; if it constitutes a new paragraph, it receives a paragraph indent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision usually made by author or editor; in designs where paragraphs are flush-left and separated by space, the distinction may be signaled by additional spacing before new paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry extract formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more lines of verse are best set off as an extract; in a note set off three or more lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry extracts are often visually centered relative to the longest line or indented uniformly for long/blank-verse extracts. Leave a half to full line of space between stanzas; reproduce the original indentation pattern; distinguish runover lines by indenting them (one em). For run-in poetry (if necessary), separate lines with a slash with a space on either side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-mark conventions (double vs single and block-quotation internal quotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted words run into the text are enclosed in double quotation marks; single quotation marks enclose quotations within quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the UK the reverse convention is common (single outer, double inner). Material set off as block quotations is not enclosed in outer quotation marks, but quoted matter within the block is enclosed in double quotation marks. Converting between run-in and block requires adding or deleting quotation marks and adjusting internal marks accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations across multiple paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted material of more than one paragraph should be presented as a block quotation if at all possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If run in for some reason, place an opening quotation mark at the beginning of the quotation and at the beginning of each new paragraph but a closing quotation mark only at the end of the final paragraph. The same practice applies to dialogue extending over paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations containing interior multi-paragraph quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted material contains an interior quotation that runs more than one paragraph, present the whole as a block quotation if possible; preserve original quotation marks except as described for permissible changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If run in, use an overall single quotation mark for the interior quotation and both double and single marks before each new paragraph within that interior quotation as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters quoted in their entirety should be set off
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter quoted in its entirety should be set off as a block quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it must be run in, include an opening quotation mark before the first line and before each new paragraph (each must begin on a new line); include a closing quotation mark only after the last line (often the signature).
